title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
current_text: A U.S. court declared Ulysses obscene while it was being published serially in The Little Review from 1918 until 1920. In October 1922, the New York Post Office Authorities seized and burned 500 copies of Ulysses during an attempt to import the novel into the United States, where its certification as obscene made importation illegal. On May 8, 1933, United States Customs seized a copy of Ulysses imported by Random House in New York as pornographic; on December 6, 1933, Judge John M. Woolsey denied the government's motion for forfeiture and destruction.

sources.quote: James Joyce’s Ulysses, one of the most important novels of the twentieth century, was declared obscene by a U.S. court while it was being published serially in the American literary magazine The Little Review from 1918 until 1920.

sources.quote:
UNITED STATES v. ONE BOOK CALLED "ULYSSES"
District Court, S.D. New York
5 F. Supp. 182
December 6, 1933
Opinion By: WOOLSEY
Opinion: [*182] WOOLSEY, District Judge.
The motion for a decree dismissing the libel herein is granted, and, consequently, of course, the
government's motion for a decree of forfeiture and destruction is denied.

ban_rows.note: UK national-level prosecution or injunction under obscenity, blasphemy, or state-secrets law. Banned in the UK after the magazine serialisation (The Egoist, 1918-1920) and book publication (Paris, 1922) were deemed obscene for the 'Nausicaa' chapter. Ban lifted in 1936 after the US ruling of 1933. Source: Wikipedia — Obscene Publications Act 1959 / Censorship in the United Kingdom / Whitehouse v Lemon / Spycatcher.
In 1920, Ulysses was banned in the United States following a prosecution for obscenity instigated by John S. Sumner, leading to the suppression of the 'Nausicaa' edition of The Little Review.
Copies were seized and destroyed at the U.S. Post Office; the ban ended with Judge Woolsey's 1933 decision and the 1934 Random House edition.
Of a 1923 print run of 500 copies sent to replace those destroyed in transit to the U.S.A., 499 are said to have been seized by the English authorities.
Banned by Nazi regime as degenerate foreign literature.
